THE TWELFTH BOOK
Treats of how the Spaniards
conquered the city
of Mexico.

To the reader.

Although many have written in Spanish about the conquest of this New Spain, according to the account of those who conquered it, it was deemed worthwhile to write it in the Mexican language—not so much to extract certain truths from the account given by the Indians themselves who took part in the conquest, as to record the vocabulary concerning matters of war and the weapons that the natives use in it, so that from this one may draw proper words and expressions for speaking in the Mexican language about this subject. It is further added that those who were conquered knew of and gave an account of many things that happened among them during the war—things unknown to those who conquered them. For these reasons, it seems to me that it has not been superfluous labor to have written this history, which was written at a time when those who took part in the very conquest were still alive; and the account was given by principal persons of sound judgment, who are held to have told the whole truth.

Twelfth Book

Book twelve of the conquest of New Spain, which is the city of Mexico.

fol. 1.

This is the twelfth book, which speaks of how war came here to this altepetl of Mexico.

Chapter first, of the signs and omens that appeared before the Spaniards came to this land, and before there was any news of them.

Chapter one: here it is told what appeared, what was seen, the sign, the omen, before the Spaniards ever arrived here upon this land, before the people here even knew of them.

Ten years before the Spaniards came to this land, there appeared in the sky a marvelous and frightful thing: it seemed to be a flame of fire, very large and very resplendent; it seemed to be stretched out across the very sky, it was wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, as when fire burns it seemed that its point reached up to the middle of the sky, and it rose—

Before the Spaniards arrived, ten years earlier, a certain omen first appeared in the heavens, like a tongue of flame, like a blaze of fire, like the glow of dawn; it seemed to be sprinkling down as it appeared; it was as though the sky itself were splitting open: wide at its base, narrow at its tip; it reached straight into the midst of the sky, to the very heart of it—

Book Twelve

The third sign or omen was that
a bolt of lightning struck the temple of
Xiuhtecuhtli, god of fire, which was

they were frightened by this because

The fourth sign or omen
was that in the daytime, while the sun
was shining, a comet fell — it appeared
as three stars together, moving in parallel,
very brightly lit, and trailing very

Book Twelve

The fifth sign or omen was that the sea of Mexico rose up, with great waves it seemed to boil, without any wind blowing, which never usually happens; without a great wind the waves came very far and entered among the houses, shaking the foundations of the houses, some houses fell, and the terror of all was great to see the water so stirred up without any wind.

The sixth sign or omen is that at night a woman's voice was heard in the air saying: "My children, now we are lost," and at times she said: "My children, where shall I take you..."

The seventh sign or omen is that the hunters of water birds caught a strange bird, about the size of a crane, and then they went to show it to Motecuçoma, who was in a hall called Tlillancalmecac; it was after midday, and [it continues]...

This is the fifth wonder: the water boiled up, not stirred by anything, it churned around, it bubbled and foamed violently, it rose very high, reaching the foundations of the houses, and shook and destroyed the houses; this was the great lake that lies here in Mexico.

[decorative border]

This is the sixth wonder: a woman was heard at night weeping and crying out loudly, going about saying: "My children, now we must go far away. Where shall I take you, my children?"

[decorative border]

This is the seventh wonder: once, when they went hunting, or were fishing upon the water, the people caught a strange, ash-colored bird like a crane; immediately they brought it to show to Motecuçoma, at Tlillan, at the calmecac, at the time when the sun was declining, in the afternoon, as...

This bird had, in the middle of its head, a round mirror, in which could be seen the sky and the stars, especially the Pleiades (the "little mast stars"), which travel near the Hyades ("the little goats"). When Motecuçoma saw this he was frightened. And the second time he looked into the mirror that the bird bore, after a little while he saw a great multitude of people gathered together, who all came armed, mounted upon horses. Then Motecuçoma ordered the soothsayers and diviners to be summoned, and asked them, "Do you not know what this is that I have seen? That many people are coming together?" But before the diviners could answer, the bird vanished, and they answered nothing.

The eighth sign or omen was that many times monsters appeared, creatures of monstrous bodies. They were brought to Motecuçoma, and as soon as he looked upon them in his chamber called Tillancalmecac, they immediately vanished.

A mirror lay upon its head, round and circular, as if it had been pierced through the middle; there could be seen the sky, the stars, and the fire-drill constellation (Mamalhuaztli). And when Motecuçoma looked upon this, he took it as a very grave omen, when he saw the stars and the fire-drill constellation. And when he looked a second time at the crown of the bird's head, he saw as though people were coming — coming gathered together, coming spread out, coming arrayed as if for war; and deer came bearing them upon their backs. Then he summoned the soothsayers, the wise men, and said to them, "Do you not know what this is that I have seen, as though people come gathered together?" But just as they were about to look upon it, it vanished, it was gone; nothing more could they say.

As for the eighth omen: many times there appeared, were shown forth, deformed people — people with two heads but one body. They were taken away, carried there to the Tlillancalmecac, and there shown to Motecuçoma; but as soon as he had seen them, they at once vanished.

Chapter two, of the first
ships that arrived at this
land: which, according to what they say, was [that of] Juan
de Grijalva.

The first time that ships appeared on the coast of this New Spain, the captains of Motecuçoma who were called Calpisques, who were stationed near the coast, immediately went to see what it was that was coming, for they had never before seen ships. One of these was the calpixqui of Cuestecatl, who was called Pinotl; he took with him other calpisques: one who was called Yaotzin, who resided in the town of Mictlan Quauhtitlan; and another who was called Teociniocatl, who resided in the town of Teociniocan; and another who was called Cuitlalpitoc. This man was not a calpisqui, but rather a servant of one of these calpisques, and a minor lord; and another minor lord who was called Tentil. These five went to see what thing that was, and they brought some things to sell, under the pretext of finding out what that thing was, and they brought with them some rich mantas, such as only Motecuçoma used, none other.

The second chapter, in which it is told how they arrived, how the first ship came: thus it is said they saw a single boat [arrive].

And it was seen that those who came arrived floating upon the heavenly waters, going along the sea, carrying with them [goods], the sea-faring merchant Pinotl, a fine calpixqui, who brought together several calpixques from Mictlan, Quauhtla, and the calpixqui Yaotzin. Third was the calpixqui from Tenanco, named Teuiacatl. Fourth was Itlalpitoc, who merely accompanied and served as a guide among them. Fifth was Tentil, who likewise served as a guide, and together these were the ones who went to see them, and who went to trade with them, going along to offer them things, to see them secretly, to spy on them: they gave them fine cloaks, precious things, indeed from the very cloak of Motecuçoma himself, which no other used, which was reserved solely for his person, for his sacred dignity: they went by sea to meet them.

Some of pleated cloth, others twisted or spiraled, others with spotted designs: all these kinds of mantas were presented to the one who went as leader among those ships that, as they say here, was Grijalva. And the Spaniards gave the Indians strings of glass beads, some green and others yellow. And when the Indians saw them they marveled greatly, and valued them highly, and took leave of the Indians saying: "Now we return to Castile, and soon we will come back, and we will go to Mexico." The Indians returned to land, and then set out for Mexico, where they arrived in one day and in one night, to bring the news to Motecuçoma of what they had seen, and they brought him the beads that the Spaniards had given them, and they spoke to him in this way: "Our lord, we are worthy of death; hear what we have seen and what we have done. We kept watch at the shore of the sea and we saw some gods within the sea, and we went to receive them, and we gave them your rich mantas; and behold here what they gave us, these beads; and they told us, if it is true that you are Mexicans, behold..."

[The messengers] then gave a report of this, and the calpixques or captains departed, and they ordered sentinels to be placed at once in the said estates. And Moctezuma then gathered his principal men: one who was called Cioacoatl, another Hilpotonqui, another Hacochalcatl, another Quappiatzin, another Tiociauacatl, another Quetzalaztatzin, another Vitznahuatlailotlac, another Hecatempatiltzin. To all of these he communicated the news that had arrived, and he showed them the glass beads that the messengers had brought, and he said to them, "It seems to me that these are precious stones; guard them carefully in the treasure-chamber so that none be lost, and if any should be lost, those who have charge of keeping the treasure-chamber shall pay for it."

That same year, in the year Thirteen Rabbit, those who were posted as sentinels saw ships at sea, and they came at once to bring word to Moctezuma with great haste. As soon as Moctezuma heard the news, he at once sent people to receive Quetzalcoatl, for he thought that it was he who was coming, because he had been expecting him every day, and since he had had word that Quetzalcoatl had gone by sea toward the east, and the ships were coming from the direction of the east, for this reason he supposed it was he. He sent five principal men to receive him and to present him with gifts, along with another gift that he had prepared beforehand. The chief among them was called Yoallichan; the second, Tepuztecatl; the third, Ticaca; the fourth, Veuetecatl; and the fifth, Vei Amecatl Heca.

Chapter 4. Of what Motecuhzoma did when he learned for the second time that the Spaniards had returned: this one was Don Hernando Cortés.

To those mentioned above Motecuhzoma spoke, and he said to them: "Look, I have been told that our lord Quetzalcoatl has arrived. Go and receive him, and do with great diligence whatever he tells you; see that nothing he says to you is forgotten. Here you have these jewels, which you shall present on my behalf, for they are all the priestly ornaments that belong to him. First, a mask worked in mosaic of turquoise. This mask had worked in the same stones a doubled and twisted serpent, whose doubling formed the tip of the nose, and whose twisting went up to the forehead like the ridge of the nose. Then the tail of the head divided, and the head together with part of the body passed over one eye, forming an eyebrow, while the tail with part of the body passed over the other eye, forming the other eyebrow. This mask was set into a tall, large crown full of rich, long, and very beautiful feathers, arranged so that when the crown was placed upon the head, the mask would be set upon the face. On the face he wore, hanging, a round, broad golden medallion, which was fastened with nine strands..."

Fourth chapter: here is told what Motecuhzoma commanded when he learned how the Spaniards had come, when they arrived for the second time — that it was Don Hernando Cortés.

He said to them: "Go, brave men, go to meet him, go to encounter our lord, go to speak with him; ask him whatever he may wish to say, whatever he may wish to take. Behold here are the personal ornaments of our lord, those of Quetzalcoatl: a serpent mask made of turquoise work, a crown of quetzal feathers, a jade breastplate lying between golden ornaments, and a shield worked with mirror-stone, arranged in matching pattern, or arranged ember-like, with a fringe of quetzal feathers, and bordered with quetzal feathers; and a mirror for the lower back, adorned with quetzal feathers. And as for that mirror for the lower back, it is covered over with turquoise, like a turquoise shield — turquoise fastened, turquoise joined, turquoise inlaid — and jade greaves, with little bells that resound. Then this is the turquoise staff, entirely of turquoise, shaped like a serpent's head."

He also wore a vest of white cloth, painted along the lower edge, and this vest was embroidered with white feathers in three bands running all the way around. He wore a rich mantle; its cloth was light blue and all worked above with many designs in very fine blue. This mantle was called tzitzilli. This mantle was put on by tying it at the waist, fastened at the corners to the body; and over this mantle there went a mosaic medallion, tied to the body over the lower back. He also wore strings of small gold bells to tie at the ankles of the feet, and likewise some white sandals such as the lords used to wear. They also carried the attire and ornaments of the god called Tlaloc Tecutli, which consisted of a mask with its plumage, like the one described above, with a banner like the one mentioned above. Also some wide earplugs of chalchihuitl (jade), which had little serpents of chalchihuitl inside them; and also a vest painted with green flowers, and some strings or a necklace of precious stones, with a medallion of precious stones. The lords and nobles of Tlaxcala entered into friendship with the Spaniards, receiving them in peace, and soon gave them rights to the royal houses, where they lodged them: and they treated them very well, administering all necessary things to them with great diligence: and they also gave them their maiden daughters, many of them, and the Spaniards received them and used them as their wives. Then the captain began to ask about Mexico, saying, "Where is Mexico? Is it far from here?" They told him: "It is not far, it is three days' journey away; it is a very populous city, and its natives are valiant and great conquerors who conquer everywhere." The Tlaxcaltecas and Cholultecas were not friends; there was discord between them, and since they wished each other ill, they spoke badly of one another to the Spaniards so that they would be mistreated, telling them that the Cholultecas were enemies and friends of the Mexicans, and as valiant as they were. The Spaniards, having heard this news about Cholollan, resolved to treat them badly, as indeed they did: they set out from Tlaxcala, all of them, together with many Cempoaltecas and Tlaxcaltecas who accompanied them, all armed for war, and arrived together at Cholollan. The Cholultecas paid no attention to any of this; they neither received them with hostility nor in peace, but remained quietly in their homes—on account of which the Spaniards formed a bad opinion of them.

[Nahuatl, parallel account:] They were led and guided [by the Cholultecas/Tlaxcaltecas], they were brought in to be lodged in their palaces; there they were greatly honored, they were given all the things that were needed, and their maidens were also given to them. Then they asked, "Where is Mexico? Is it still far away?" They answered, "It is no longer far; it will take four days; it is very good, and it is very populous, with many warriors, mountain-dwelling people; one cannot even see its mountains." But as for the Tlaxcalteca, there had been constant quarreling, anger, hatred, and envy between them, so that they could not see each other well, and the Cholulteca could never get along with them. Because of this, [the Tlaxcalteca] counseled the Spaniards to hate the Cholulteca, telling them, "They are indeed very wicked; they are treacherous like the Mexica, friends of the Mexica." Thus the Spaniards believed it, and immediately they went to Cholollan, taking with them the Tlaxcalteca and the Cempoalteca, going to make war...

[Suspecting] some treachery from them, the Spaniards immediately began calling out loudly to the lords and chiefs and all the other people, so that they would come to where the Spaniards were. They all gathered in the courtyard of the great [temple] of Quetzalcoatl.
